## Today’s goals

By the end of this session, you should be able to:

- Distinguish an editor, an extension, and an AI agent.
- Explain the role of VS Code Insiders.
- Compare VS Code, Zed, Qoder, and Positron.
- Choose a tool for a data-science or software workflow.
- Evaluate model access, privacy, and review controls.
- Run the same bounded task across multiple editors.

## Start with the layers

```text
Editor or IDE
  ├─ language support and debugger
  ├─ terminal and version control
  ├─ extensions
  └─ AI interface
       ├─ model/provider
       ├─ repository context
       └─ tools, permissions, and agent loop
```

Changing editors does not automatically change the model. Installing an extension can change what code and data a provider receives.

## VS Code {.compact}

[Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/) is a general-purpose, open-source-based editor with a large extension ecosystem.

Its current AI surfaces include:

- Chat and inline assistance
- Agent and planning workflows
- Workspace instructions and skills
- Tool and MCP integrations
- Diff review and change reversal
- Multiple agent harnesses and models where configured

Capabilities depend on installed extensions, account entitlements, and organizational policy.

## Extensions are code you trust

An extension may be able to:

- Read workspace files
- Run commands
- Connect to external services
- Access tokens granted to the editor
- Modify settings or source files
- Install additional components

Before installing, inspect the publisher, permissions, repository, update history, privacy terms, and workspace-trust behavior. More extensions are not automatically better.

## VS Code Insiders

[VS Code Insiders](https://code.visualstudio.com/insiders/) is the daily pre-release build of VS Code.

Use it to:

- Try features before the stable release
- Test extension compatibility
- Follow rapidly changing AI interfaces
- Maintain a separate experimental setup

Expect more change and occasional regressions. Keep stable VS Code for important work unless pre-release testing is the purpose.

## Zed {.compact}

[Zed](https://zed.dev/) is a high-performance collaborative code editor with integrated AI workflows.

Its AI interface emphasizes:

- Agentic editing
- Real-time visibility into agent navigation
- Editable unified diffs
- Accept/reject review
- External agents through the Agent Client Protocol
- MCP integrations

Confirm platform availability, provider support, and current plan details for your environment.

## Qoder

[Qoder](https://qoder.com/) presents itself as an agentic coding platform with editor, CLI, plugin, and task-oriented experiences.

Evaluation questions:

- Can it use the required language tooling?
- Which models and accounts are supported?
- What repository context is uploaded?
- How are commands approved and isolated?
- Can all changes be reviewed as a diff?
- Can the task be reproduced outside Qoder?

Product claims should be tested on your own representative task.

## Positron {.compact}

[Positron](https://posit.co/products/ide/positron/) is a data-science IDE from Posit, built from the Code OSS ecosystem and designed around Python and R.

Its differentiators include:

- R and Python interpreters
- Data Explorer and variable views
- Integrated plots, help, and console workflows
- Notebook and source-file support
- Data-science-oriented language tooling
- AI assistance through supported features and extensions

For statistical teaching, the language and data workflow may matter more than raw agent autonomy.

## Comparison by primary emphasis {.compact}

| Tool | Primary emphasis | Useful starting audience |
|---|---|---|
| VS Code | Extensible general development | Broad language and extension needs |
| VS Code Insiders | Early feature testing | Evaluators and extension developers |
| Zed | Fast collaborative editor + agents | Developers wanting native-speed review |
| Qoder | Agentic project/task workflow | Users testing higher-level delegation |
| Positron | R/Python data science | Analysts, instructors, and researchers |

These are starting points, not a benchmark result.

## Compare workflows, not screenshots {.compact}

Run the same small task in each candidate:

> In a copy of this project, add a test for one known edge case, make the minimum fix, run the focused test, and show the final diff. Do not install packages or edit unrelated files.

Record:

- Time to correct result
- Number and scope of edits
- Approval prompts
- Test evidence
- Ease of reviewing and reverting
- Provider and account cost

## Data-science evaluation task

For R or Python, try:

1. Open a versioned project.
2. Select the correct interpreter or environment.
3. Load a public dataset.
4. Ask the assistant to explain—then minimally modify—one plot.
5. Run the file from a clean session.
6. Inspect variables, plots, and generated artifacts.
7. Revert the change.

An IDE succeeds only if the environment and result are reproducible.

## Privacy and institutional policy

Ask before enabling AI:

- Is code retained or used for training?
- Which provider receives context?
- Can the extension index the entire repository?
- Are excluded files truly excluded from requests?
- Where are credentials stored?
- Can telemetry be controlled?
- Is the product approved for student or research data?

Do not infer policy compliance from an education discount or “enterprise” label.

## Avoid the extension pile-up

Multiple overlapping assistants can create:

- Competing completions and keybindings
- Duplicate repository indexing
- Unclear model billing
- Conflicting edits
- Larger attack surface
- Difficulty identifying which service sent data

Enable one assistant at a time during evaluation and document the configuration.

## Demo roadmap

1. Show the same repository in stable VS Code and Positron.
2. Compare R/Python environment selection.
3. Show VS Code Insiders as a separate test installation.
4. Run one read-only explanation in Zed or Qoder.
5. Request one tiny change.
6. Inspect the diff and command log.
7. Run the same test externally.
8. Revert the change.

## Mini-activity: choose the environment

Choose a starting tool for each scenario and defend the choice:

1. An introductory R course with tables and plots
2. A polyglot web project with many extensions
3. Testing next month’s VS Code API
4. Pairing with an external ACP agent
5. Evaluating autonomous implementation tasks

Name one reason your choice might still be wrong.

## Key takeaways

- The editor, AI extension, model, and tool permissions are separate choices.
- VS Code prioritizes breadth; Insiders previews change; Positron centers R/Python data science.
- Zed and Qoder offer different agent-oriented workflows that require hands-on evaluation.
- Compare candidates with the same bounded task, clean environment, and review criteria.
- Minimize overlapping extensions and verify privacy, cost, diffs, tests, and rollback.
